How OBD-2 works, in plain words
Your bike\'s fuel injection is run by a small computer (the ECU). It checks the engine\'s sensors all the time: oxygen sensor, temperatures, throttle and more.

When something goes wrong, it turns on the check-engine light on your dash and saves a code that says what went wrong, like P0301 for a misfire. The light only says something is wrong; the code says what.

OBD-2 is the standard way to read these codes. It is mandatory on new two-wheelers in India (OBD-2A from 2023, the stricter OBD-2B from 2025). It is not one sensor: it is the bike\'s self-check system plus a socket to read it.
A Bluetooth OBD-2 adapter: a thumb-sized plug that goes into the bike\'s diagnostic socket and talks to your phone over Bluetooth. It can stay plugged in.
The socket is usually under the rider seat or near the battery. Bikes often use a smaller socket than cars, so you may also need a short adapter cable.
Before buying, send a photo of your bike\'s socket (task 3 in docs/YOUR-TASKS.txt), so the right adapter and cable can be picked.
Plug the adapter into the bike\'s diagnostic socket.
Turn the ignition on (engine can be off or running).
In this app: Bike tab → Find adapter → tap your adapter. The top bar turns green: OBD connected.
The bike\'s self-check found nothing wrong.
A stored fault code, with a description below it. Show it to your service centre. If the check-engine light is on, this is why.
The computer noticed a problem once and is watching it. Nothing to panic about, but mention it at your next service.
Early warning signs in live data
Battery: about 12.4–12.8 V with the engine off and 13.5–14.5 V running is normal. Below 12 V with the engine off, or below 13 V running, points to a weak battery or charging problem.
Engine temp: a liquid-cooled engine normally settles around 80–100 °C. Much higher, especially in traffic, means stop and let it cool, and have the coolant checked.
